item.title: Development and Validation of a Pre-COPD Score to Predict Incident COPD
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: The ability to predict progression from a pre-disease state in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), pre-COPD, to overt COPD remains limited.

Objective: To test the hypothesis that development of COPD can be predicted by characterizing pre-COPD and creating a simple pre-COPD score.

Methods: We identified individuals without airflow obstruction, defined as pre-bronchodilator (BD) forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1)/forced vital capacity (FVC)≥0.70 and ≥lower limit of normal, from the Copenhagen General Population Study (CGPS)(N = 14,506), Copenhagen City Heart Study (CCHS)(N = 8673), and Genetic Epidemiology for COPD (COPDGene) Study(N = 2982). A pre-COPD score was developed in CGPS by assigning 1 point to each of smoking history≥10 pack-years, active smoking, any respiratory symptom, asthma, and pre-BD FEV1/FVC 0.70-0.75, and 4 points for pre-BD FEV1<80% predicted, indicating presence of Preserved Ratio Impaired Spirometry (PRISm), with external validation in CCHS and COPDGene. Participants were followed for 5-10 years for incident COPD, defined as pre-BD FEV1/FVC<0.70 and FEV1<80% predicted.

Measurements and main results: During follow-up, COPD developed in 669 individuals (4.6%) in CGPS, 685 (7.9%) in CCHS, and 367 (12%) in COPDGene. In CGPS, 10-year incidence was 1.5% in the low-risk, 9.3% in the intermediate-risk, 24% in the high-risk, and 42% in the very high-risk category. Corresponding 5-year incidences were 3.7%, 7.3%, 12%, and 25% in CCHS, and 4.1%, 5.3%, 13%, and 31% in COPDGene, respectively. The pre-COPD score demonstrated good discrimination with areas under curve of 0.88 in CGPS, 0.76 in CCHS, and 0.81 in COPDGene. The pre-COPD score was also associated with exacerbations.

Conclusions: The pre-COPD score is useful in predicting the onset of COPD with clinically relevant discrimination in three cohorts with different risk profiles.

item.title: Reduced desaturation-based detection of sleep apnea events in self-identified Black individuals across two cohorts
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Pulse oximetry may overestimate oxygen saturation in individuals with darker skin pigmentation, potentially reducing detection of desaturation during sleep-disordered breathing.

Objectives: To assess racial/ethnic differences in desaturation-based obstructive event detection and cardiovascular risk, and evaluate heart-rate response as an oximetry-independent marker for risk stratification.

Methods: We analyzed participants without cardiovascular disease in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis(MESA) and Sleep Heart Health Study(SHHS). We modeled desaturation-based AHI relative to airflow-defined AHI and examined AHI-ΔHR6, defined by respiratory events with a heart-rate increase ≥6 beats/min. Adjusted Cox models evaluated associations with a composite outcome, major adverse cardiovascular events or all-cause mortality(MACE/mortality).

Measurements and main results: Black participants had 21% and 20% lower proportions of airflow-defined events meeting the ≥4% desaturation criterion than White participants in MESA (ratio 0.79[95% CI,0.68-0.93]; p = 0.003) and SHHS (0.80[0.68-0.94]; p = 0.008), respectively. No other racial/ethnic group showed a lower proportion of airflow-defined events meeting desaturation criteria than White participants. AHI-ΔHR6 event detection was similar between Black and White participants in both cohorts. In Whites participants, desaturation-based events were associated with MACE/mortality in MESA but not in SHHS, while desaturation-based AHI measures were not significantly associated with MACE/mortality in Black individuals in either cohort. In contrast, AHI-ΔHR6 was associated with MACE/mortality in MESA (HR 1.33[1.09-1.63];p=0.006) and SHHS (1.26[1.02-1.55]; p = 0.033).

Conclusions: Desaturation-based scoring identified a lower proportion of reduced flow events in Black than White participants, whereas heart-rate-response-based event detection was similar across groups, suggesting oximetry-related under-detection in individuals with darker pigment.

item.title: As-needed inhaled corticosteroids in asthma: an Official American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Background: Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing reliever therapy has demonstrated efficacy in improving asthma outcomes when compared to short-acting beta2-agonists (SABA) alone but remains underutilized. The purpose of this guideline is to provide recommendations surrounding the use of combination ICS-formoterol or ICS+SABA (in combination or separate inhalers) as reliever therapy across the asthma severity spectrum in adolescents and adults.

Methods: The American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline panel evaluated six research questions in the PICO format addressing the use of ICS-containing reliever therapy across National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) asthma treatment steps 1-5. The methodology team conducted systematic literature reviews and GRADE assessments, which the panel utilized to inform the recommendations for each specific PICO and overall.

Recommendations: In patients at NAEPP steps 1 and 2, the panel made strong recommendations for the use of as-needed-only ICS-SABA or ICS-formoterol over SABA-only therapy, and conditional recommendations over scheduled ICS + as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5, the taskforce made a strong recommendation for the use of maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) with ICS-formoterol over scheduled ICS-LABA plus as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5 who are using scheduled maintenance ICS-LABA, the panel made a conditional recommendation for use of ICS+SABA reliever over SABA reliever. In considering these recommendations, the panel valued the importance of preventing severe exacerbations and considered the risk of SABA-only treatment, as well as ICS and systemic corticosteroid (SCS) exposure.

Conclusions: This clinical practice guideline, informed by systematic reviews and GRADE-based appraisals of PICO-framed evidence, makes these evidence-based recommendations for the safe and effective use of ICS-containing reliever therapy in asthma.

item.title: Lung Allograft Function After Primary Graft Dysfunction in the Lung Transplant Outcomes Group Cohort
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Primary graft dysfunction (PGD) after lung transplant is associated with increased mortality. Whether PGD increases mortality via long-term effects on allograft function is poorly understood.

Objective: Evaluate the association of PGD with potential lung function and chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD).

Methods: We included lung transplant recipients enrolled in an 8-center prospective cohort study from 2007-2018. PGD was defined by ISHLT criteria. Linear mixed effects and logistic regression models evaluated the association between PGD and maximum potential forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and whether Global Lung Function Initiative defined (GLI) predicted FEV1 was attained, respectively. Flexible parametric survival models evaluated the association between PGD and CLAD, accounting for confounding and mortality as a competing risk.

Measurements and main results: Among 2419 recipients, 510 had PGD. Recipients with PGD had lower maximum potential FEV1 (-311 ml, 95% CI -245 to -377 ml) and were less likely to achieve GLI-predicted FEV1 (probability difference -12.5%, 95% CI -17 to -8%). 930 recipients developed CLAD (405 obstructive, 525 restrictive) over median (IQR) 5.9 (3.0-8.0 years). The 5-year cumulative incidence of CLAD did not differ by PGD (cumulative difference: -2.2%, 95% CI - 6.4% to 1.9%). This association was not modified by age, sex, BMI, pretransplant diagnosis, or transplant type. PGD was not associated with a difference in cumulative incidence of obstructive or restrictive CLAD (cumulative difference -1.2% and -0.8%, respectively).

Conclusion: PGD is associated with reduced lung function and lower likelihood of achieving GLI-predicted maximum potential lung function but not CLAD.

item.title: Dupilumab is associated with improved lung functions in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation: a post hoc analysis of the BOREAS and NOTUS trials
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Type 2 inflammation is present in 20%-40% of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Objective: To perform in-depth analyses of the efficacy of dupilumab on lung function parameters in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation.

Methods: In BOREAS (NCT03930732) and NOTUS (NCT04456673), patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation were randomized to dupilumab 300 mg (n = 938) or placebo (n = 936) subcutaneously every 2 weeks for 52 weeks.

Measurements and main results: Dupilumab versus placebo improved pre-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1; least squares mean difference: 83 [95% confidence interval (CI): 53-112] mL; P < .0001), post-bronchodilator FEV1 (71 [41-101] mL; P < .0001), pre-bronchodilator forced vital capacity (FVC; 64 [26-102] mL; P = .0009), post-bronchodilator FVC (41 [3-79] mL; P = .0341), post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC (0.016 [0.010-0.022]; P < .0001), and forced expiratory flow 25%-75% of FVC (78 [45-111] mL/s; P < .0001) at week 12 and sustained to week 52. Improvements in pre-bronchodilator FEV1 were observed regardless of smoking status or the presence of co-existing emphysema; greater improvements were observed in patients with higher baseline eosinophil counts or fractional exhaled nitric oxide. Dupilumab versus placebo achieved >100 mL improvements in pre-bronchodilator FEV1 at week 12 (42.2% vs 31.1%) and week 52 (36.9% vs 31.2%), with a similar proportion for post-bronchodilator FEV1 at weeks 12 and 52.

Conclusions: Dupilumab treatment resulted in early and sustained improvements across multiple spirometric lung function parameters in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation.
